title: Testing one trading rule on hundreds of tickers

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Here's a strange result. A trading rule turned a coin called OMGUSD into about a 200 percent gain, while simply holding it lost around 80 percent. How does a rule do that?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: By betting against the fall, I'd guess. Where does this come from?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: From Antoine's BatchBacktesting engine, run at portfolio scale. Instead of testing one stock, he runs a rule across the whole S and P 500 and every crypto pair, and compares the results.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Why bother with so many? One ticker is easier to read.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Because one ticker tells you whether the rule worked once. A big grid shows whether it works across sectors and eras, and where it falls apart. It's like testing a recipe in a hundred kitchens instead of one.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Two classics, built with backtesting dot py and pandas T A. The first is an EMA crossover: buy when the 20-period average crosses above the 80-period one, sell on the opposite cross, with a ten percent stop loss and a twenty-five percent take profit. The second is MACD: buy when the MACD line crosses above its signal line, sell on the reverse.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And the machinery to run all of that?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Data adapters pull prices from Financial Modeling Prep and Binance. Strategy objects hold the parameters. A runner fans the work across a thread pool, twelve threads in his example, and writes CSV files and optional charts.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What did the leaderboard look like?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: For the EMA rule, the top five ranged from about 194 percent up to 294 percent, with BTCBUSD in first place at roughly 294. Next to each result, the charts show buy-and-hold for the same instrument, which is the comparison that makes the numbers meaningful.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the OMGUSD case is the interesting one.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. The rule made money by being short through a collapse, while Bitcoin and ALB rose under both approaches. That's what a wide run reveals: which gains come from the rule and which come from the period.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And how do you compare the two strategies fairly?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Look at the median return across all tickers, not just the top five. That's a sturdier yardstick. The takeaway: a multi-ticker run is a great smoke test for a rule. The full write-up has both strategies' code and the leaderboards.
